phases: 2. Symbolic Execution (AI-simulated path analysis for all public/external functions)
3. Fuzz Testing Coverage (forge fuzz 256 runs per property)
4. Access Control Verification (role hierarchy, modifier analysis, privilege escalation)
5. Economic Attack Vector Analysis (MEV, sandwich, governance, rate-limit bypass)
7. Reentrancy Deep Analysis (CEI pattern, cross-function, cross-contract)
10. Gas Optimization (storage layout, cold writes, redundant SLOADS)
12. Event Emission Completeness (state-change coverage, indexed params)
14. Deployment Security (constructor args, CREATE2, key management)
15. Centralization Risk Assessment (owner powers, operator control, pause implications)

findings.title: Reentrancy in BridgeLock.initiateBurnRelease — State writes after external call
findings.description: BridgeLock.initiateBurnRelease() calls wbait.burnFrom() (external call) at line 179, then writes state (burnReleases mapping, burnReleaseIds array) at lines 181-186. Although the nonReentrant modifier is present, this violates the Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern. If WBAIT._update() had any callback mechanism (e.g., ERC-777 hooks), reentrancy would be exploitable. Currently mitigated by nonReentrant + Pausable, but the pattern is fragile against future WBAIT modifications.
findings.recommendation: Reorder to follow CEI pattern: save state variables before the external call to wbait.burnFrom(). Consider adding a reentrancy guard at the WBAIT level as defense-in-depth.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Mitigated by nonReentrant modifier; fix recommended for defense-in-depth
findings.exploit_scenario: If WBAIT is upgraded to ERC-777 or implements hooks, an attacker could reenter initiateBurnRelease to create duplicate BurnRelease entries with the same burn amount, potentially enabling double-release on L1.

findings.title: Unchecked return value of wbait.approve() in BAITUniswapV3Liquidity.addLiquidity
findings.description: The return value of wbait.approve(address(positionManager), amountWBAIT) at line 111 is ignored. While ERC-20 approve() from OpenZeppelin returns bool and should always return true, non-standard ERC-20 tokens or tokens that return false on failure would silently fail here. The position manager would then attempt to transfer wBAIT without approval, causing the mint to revert with an uninformative error.
findings.recommendation: Use SafeERC20.safeApprove() or require() on the return value: `require(wbait.approve(address(positionManager), amountWBAIT), "approve failed");`. Alternatively, use forceApprove pattern from OpenZeppelin 5.x.
findings.status: OPEN — Should be fixed before mainnet deployment
findings.exploit_scenario: If wBAIT ever returns false on approve (e.g., due to a bug in a future upgrade), addLiquidity would silently proceed with zero approval, causing positionManager.mint() to revert with confusing error.

findings.title: Missing zero-address validation for _weth in BAITUniswapV3Liquidity constructor
findings.description: The constructor does not validate that _weth != address(0). If zero address is passed, createPool() and addLiquidity() will interact with address(0), causing irreversible failures. Unlike _wbait which is validated in WBAIT, and _wbait in BridgeLock, this parameter has no zero-check.
findings.recommendation: Add `require(_weth != address(0), "BAITUniswapV3Liquidity: zero WETH address");` in constructor. Also validate _factory and _positionManager.
findings.status: OPEN — Easy fix, should be patched

findings.title: block.timestamp used for rate limiting — manipulable by validators
findings.description: BridgeLock.requestLockMint() uses `block.timestamp / 1 days` for rate limiting at line 108. Miners/validators can manipulate block.timestamp within ~15 seconds. This allows slight boundary manipulation: a validator could push a timestamp across the day boundary to reset the dailyMinted counter early, enabling up to 2x rate limit in a single 'day' (at the boundary). With 100K wBAIT/day, this is a potential ~100K extra mint per boundary event.
findings.recommendation: This is an inherent limitation of on-chain time-based rate limiting. Mitigations: (1) Use block.number instead (less manipulable, less intuitive), (2) Use Chainlink or similar oracle for timestamp, (3) Accept the ~15s drift as acceptable risk given 24h windows. Document the ~0.017% drift as acceptable.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Inherent to on-chain rate limiting; ~15s drift is acceptable for 24h windows

findings.title: Rate limit applies per-recipient but not globally — 5x multiplier via operator coordination
findings.description: The rate limit (100K wBAIT/day) is per-recipient address, not global. Five operators could submit requests for five different recipients, each getting 100K/day, for a total of 500K wBAIT/day. This is by design (per-address rate limiting), but may not match the intended security model if the goal was to limit total bridge throughput.
findings.recommendation: Add an optional global daily mint limit if total bridge throughput should be capped. Current per-recipient limit is a reasonable design choice but should be explicitly documented as allowing N*100K/day total throughput across N unique recipients.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Design decision; document per-recipient vs global rate limit semantics

findings.title: No timelock implementation for operator updates despite TIMELOCK_DURATION constant
findings.description: BridgeLock declares `TIMELOCK_DURATION = 24 hours` but there is no function to update operators with a timelock delay. The OperatorUpdated event exists (line 67) but no function emits it. Operator changes are currently impossible after deployment — operators are set in the constructor and immutable. This means if an operator key is compromised, there is NO on-chain mechanism to replace it. This is a critical governance gap.
findings.recommendation: Implement operator update with 24h timelock: (1) `proposeOperatorUpdate(uint256 index, address newOp)` — starts timelock, (2) `executeOperatorUpdate(uint256 index, address newOp)` — executes after TIMELOCK_DURATION. This is essential for production operations.
findings.status: OPEN — Critical governance gap; must be addressed before mainnet

findings.title: WBAIT.bridgeLock is immutable — cannot update if BridgeLock is compromised or upgraded
findings.description: WBAIT.bridgeLock is declared as `immutable` (line 19), meaning it is set once in the constructor and cannot be changed. If BridgeLock is compromised, has a critical bug, or needs upgrading, WBAIT must be redeployed entirely. This creates a single-point-of-failure dependency.
findings.recommendation: Consider making bridgeLock a mutable state variable with a timelocked update mechanism (e.g., 48h timelock). Trade-off: mutability adds governance risk but enables emergency response. Alternative: use a proxy pattern for BridgeLock so the implementation can be upgraded while the address stays the same.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Design choice; document the immutable commitment and emergency recovery plan (redeploy WBAIT)

findings.title: Solidity 0.8.20 has known compiler bugs
findings.description: Solidity 0.8.20 has 3 known bugs: (1) VerbatimInvalidDeduplication — invalid deduplication of verbatim functions, (2) FullInlinerNonExpressionSplitting — full inliner may produce incorrect code when non-expression splitting is used, (3) MissingSideEffectsOnSelectorAccess — missing side effects on selector access. While these may not affect current code, they represent compiler-level risk.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to Solidity 0.8.28+ which fixes all known bugs. Pin exact version (remove caret ^) to prevent accidental compilation with buggy versions. Add `pragma solidity 0.8.28;` (exact).
findings.status: OPEN — Should upgrade before mainnet

findings.title: initiateBurnRelease burns entire balance without user-specified amount
findings.description: BridgeLock.initiateBurnRelease() burns `wbait.balanceOf(msg.sender)` — the user's ENTIRE wBAIT balance. There is no amount parameter. This means a user cannot partially bridge back to L1; they must bridge all or nothing. If a user has wBAIT from multiple sources and only wants to bridge a portion, they must first transfer the unwanted portion to another address, then call initiateBurnRelease.
findings.recommendation: Add an `amount` parameter: `function initiateBurnRelease(uint256 amount, string calldata l1ReleaseAddress)`. Validate `amount <= wbait.balanceOf(msg.sender)`. This provides flexibility and reduces unnecessary transfer operations.
findings.status: OPEN — UX limitation; add amount parameter

findings.title: No approval check before burnFrom — initiateBurnRelease will revert if allowance insufficient
findings.description: BridgeLock.initiateBurnRelease() calls `wbait.burnFrom(msg.sender, amount)` at line 179. burnFrom requires the caller (BridgeLock) to have allowance from msg.sender. Users must first call `wbait.approve(address(bridgeLock), amount)`. This is a foot-gun: if a user forgets to approve, the transaction reverts with no clear error message. Additionally, ERC20Permit (EIP-2612) is available on WBAIT but not leveraged in the burn flow.
findings.recommendation: Option 1: Document the approve requirement clearly. Option 2: Add a `initiateBurnReleaseWithPermit()` function that accepts a permit signature, combining approve+burn in one transaction. This eliminates the two-tx UX and reduces gas.
findings.status: OPEN — Add permit-based burn flow for better UX

findings.title: amount0Min/amount1Min set to 0 in addLiquidity — sandwich attack vulnerability
findings.description: BAITUniswapV3Liquidity.addLiquidity() sets amount0Min=0 and amount1Min=0 (lines 121-122). This means there is no minimum amount protection. A MEV attacker can sandwich the liquidity addition: front-run with a price move, let the liquidity be added at the unfavorable price, then back-run to profit. The owner adding liquidity during pool creation is especially vulnerable.
findings.recommendation: Set amount0Min and amount1Min to reasonable slippage tolerances (e.g., 95-99% of desired amounts). For pool creation where the owner controls the initial price, 1-2% slippage tolerance is appropriate. Use deadline check (already present at line 124) as additional protection.
findings.status: OPEN — Must fix for mainnet; zero slippage protection is dangerous

findings.title: LockRequest duplicate prevention relies on confirmations == 0 check — collision risk
findings.description: BridgeLock.requestLockMint() checks `lockRequests[requestId].confirmations == 0` to prevent duplicate requests (line 104). If a request is created and then the storage is somehow cleared (which shouldn't happen in normal operation but is a theoretical concern), the same requestId could be reused. More practically, the requestId is operator-chosen, so two operators could independently try to create the same requestId with different parameters — only the first succeeds, but the second's transaction reverts unexpectedly.
findings.recommendation: Add a dedicated `bool exists` field to LockRequest struct instead of relying on confirmations == 0 as a proxy. This is more explicit and prevents any edge-case confusion.
findings.status: LOW PRIORITY — Current approach works but is implicit

findings.title: No mechanism to cancel a pending LockRequest or BurnRelease
findings.description: Once a LockRequest is submitted (with 1-2 confirmations), there is no way to cancel it before it reaches 3 confirmations and executes. If operators discover a fraudulent or erroneous request, they can only refuse to confirm it — the request stays pending forever. Similarly, BurnReleases cannot be cancelled. This could lead to accumulation of stale/fraudulent requests.
findings.recommendation: Add `cancelLockMint(bytes32 requestId)` callable by any operator after a timeout (e.g., 7 days) or by the original requester. Add `cancelBurnRelease(bytes32 releaseId)` for the burner. Requires careful design to prevent griefing.
findings.status: OPEN — Should implement for operational safety

findings.title: OperatorUpdated event has unindexed address parameters
findings.description: The OperatorUpdated(uint256 index, address oldOp, address newOp) event at line 67 has address parameters that are not indexed. Indexing oldOp and newOp would enable efficient filtering for operator change history, which is critical for governance monitoring and off-chain audit trails.
findings.recommendation: Change to: `event OperatorUpdated(uint256 indexed index, address indexed oldOp, address indexed newOp);`. Note: max 3 indexed parameters per event, this uses exactly 3.
findings.status: OPEN — Minor but improves observability

findings.title: WETH variable not in mixedCase (naming convention)
findings.description: The immutable variable `WETH` in BAITUniswapV3Liquidity (line 62) uses all-caps, which is the convention for constants, not immutables. While WETH is a well-known address convention in DeFi, Slither flags this as a naming violation.
findings.recommendation: Rename to `weth` (mixedCase) for consistency with Solidity style guide. WETH is commonly used in DeFi interfaces, so this is acceptable as-is, but `weth` is more technically correct for an immutable.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — WETH naming is a DeFi convention; acceptable

findings.title: Reentrancy-benign in initiateBurnRelease — external call to burnFrom before event emission
findings.description: Slither identifies benign reentrancy in initiateBurnRelease where the external call to wbait.burnFrom() could theoretically emit events from WBAIT before the BurnInitiated event from BridgeLock. This is event-ordering concern, not a security risk.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Event ordering is not security-critical.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — No security impact

findings.title: Reentrancy-events in BAITUniswapV3Liquidity.createPool and addLiquidity
findings.description: External calls to Uniswap V3 factory and position manager could emit events before the contract's own events. This is an event-ordering issue, not a security vulnerability.
findings.recommendation: No action required for security. For consistent event ordering in off-chain indexers, consider emitting events before external calls (where possible).
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Event ordering only

findings.title: Deployment script uses temporary bridgeLock address pattern
findings.description: DeployBAIT.s.sol deploys WBAIT with `msg.sender` as bridgeLock (line 25), then deploys BridgeLock. The deployer temporarily has mint power. The comment mentions CREATE2 for production but it's not implemented. If the deployer is compromised between deployment steps, they could mint unlimited tokens.
findings.recommendation: Implement CREATE2 pre-computation: compute BridgeLock address before deploying WBAIT, then deploy WBAIT with the pre-computed address. This eliminates the window where deployer has mint power. Alternative: deploy in a single atomic transaction using a factory contract.
findings.status: OPEN — Implement CREATE2 or factory pattern for production deployment

findings.title: Test suite has incomplete coverage — no integration tests for lock-mint-burn cycle
findings.description: BAIT.t.sol tests 8 WBAIT functions and 3 BridgeLock functions. Missing tests: (1) Full 3-of-5 confirmation flow, (2) Rate limit enforcement, (3) Pause behavior under bridge operations, (4) Burn-release flow, (5) Supply cap edge cases, (6) Multiple concurrent lock requests, (7) Operator management.
findings.recommendation: Expand test suite to achieve >95% line coverage and 100% branch coverage. Add invariant tests (forge invariant) for: totalSupply <= MAX_SUPPLY, dailyMinted[addr] <= RATE_LIMIT, lockRequests[reqId].confirmations <= NUM_OPERATORS.
findings.status: OPEN — Critical for production; current coverage is insufficient

findings.title: burnReleaseId collision theoretically possible
findings.description: The burnReleaseId is computed as `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, amount, block.number, burnReleaseIds.length))`. While collision is extremely unlikely, if the same user burns the same amount in the same block (via different transactions), and the array length counter is somehow manipulated, IDs could collide. The nonReentrant modifier prevents same-tx reentry but not same-block different-tx scenarios.
findings.recommendation: Add block.timestamp or a nonce to the hash: `keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, amount, block.number, block.timestamp, burnReleaseIds.length))`. Alternatively, use a sequential counter.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Extremely low probability; adding block.timestamp is a cheap mitigation

findings.title: No event emission for pause/unpause in BridgeLock
findings.description: BridgeLock.pause() and unpause() (lines 212-213) do not emit custom events. While OpenZeppelin's Pausable emits Paused/Unpaused events, custom events with contract-specific context would improve auditability.
findings.recommendation: OpenZeppelin 5.x Pausable already emits Paused(address) and Unpaused(address) events. This is sufficient but custom events with more context (reason, timestamp) could be useful.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — OZ5 Pausable events are sufficient

findings.title: Multiple Solidity versions across project (pragma inconsistency)
findings.description: The project uses ^0.8.20 for contracts but forge-std uses >=0.8.13<0.9.0. This version inconsistency could lead to subtle compilation differences.
findings.recommendation: Pin exact Solidity version in all contracts and foundry.toml. Use `pragma solidity 0.8.28;` (no caret).
findings.status: OPEN — Pin exact version

findings.title: forge-std unused state variables in test/script contracts
findings.description: Slither reports 25 instances of unused-state variables from forge-std's CommonBase (CONSOLE, DEFAULT_SENDER, MULTICALL3_ADDRESS, UINT256_MAX, SECP256K1_ORDER, DEFAULT_TEST_CONTRACT, CREATE2_FACTORY, stdstore) and ScriptBase (vmSafe). These are inherited but never used in the test and script contracts.
findings.recommendation: These are false positives from forge-std's design. No action required. Can be suppressed in slither.config.json.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — False positives from forge-std

findings.title: Test function naming not in mixedCase (Foundry convention)
findings.description: Foundry test functions use test_ prefix with PascalCase (e.g., test_Pause, test_MaxSupply). This violates Solidity naming convention but is Foundry's standard practice.
findings.recommendation: No action required. Foundry convention overrides Solidity style guide for test functions.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Foundry convention

findings.title: External calls inside loop in BridgeLockTest.test_OperatorCount
findings.description: The test function calls bridgeLock.isOperator() inside a for loop. This is a gas concern in production code but acceptable in tests.
findings.recommendation: No action required in test code.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Test code only

findings.title: Unchecked transfer return value in test code
findings.description: WBAITTest.test_Pause() ignores the return value of wbait.transfer(). This is acceptable in test code but would be a real issue in production code.
findings.recommendation: No action required in test code. Production code should use SafeERC20.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Test code only

findings.title: Owner single-point-of-failure — both WBAIT and BridgeLock use single-owner pattern
findings.description: Both WBAIT and BridgeLock inherit Ownable2Step with a single owner. The owner can: (1) pause/unpause WBAIT (freezing all transfers), (2) pause/unpause BridgeLock (freezing all bridge operations), (3) createPool and addLiquidity. If the owner key is compromised, the attacker can permanently freeze the bridge and all token transfers. Ownable2Step adds protection for ownership transfer (2-step) but not for the owner's operational powers.
findings.recommendation: Replace single-owner with a timelocked multisig (e.g., Gnosis Safe 3-of-5 + 48h TimelockController) for production. At minimum, add a 24h timelock on pause operations. Consider using AccessControl with multiple roles instead of single owner.
findings.status: OPEN — Must address for mainnet; single-owner is a centralization risk

findings.title: Emergency pause has no timelock or multi-sig requirement — owner can rug via pause
findings.description: WBAIT.pause() freezes ALL transfers (the _update override enforces whenNotPaused). BridgeLock.pause() freezes ALL bridge operations. There is no timelock on pause, no multisig requirement, and no automatic unpause mechanism. A compromised or malicious owner can instantly and permanently freeze the entire system with no recourse for users.
findings.recommendation: Implement: (1) Timelock on pause (e.g., 4h delay), (2) Auto-unpause after max duration (e.g., 72h), (3) Require 2-of-5 operators to approve pause, (4) Emit detailed event with pause reason, (5) Add circuit-breaker pattern that pauses only specific functions (e.g., pause mint but allow burn).
findings.status: OPEN — Critical centralization risk

findings.title: No on-chain conservation invariant enforcement — totalSupply vs totalLockedOnL1
findings.description: The documentation states the conservation invariant: totalSupply == totalLockedOnL1. However, there is no on-chain variable tracking totalLockedOnL1 or enforcement mechanism. The invariant depends entirely on correct off-chain L1 monitoring and operator behavior. If operators mint without corresponding L1 locks (maliciously or by error), the invariant is broken with no on-chain detection.
findings.recommendation: Add a `uint256 public totalLockedOnL1` counter to BridgeLock. Increment on lock-mint execution, decrement on burn-release confirmation. Add an invariant check function: `function verifyConservationInvariant() external view returns (bool) { return wbait.totalSupply() == totalLockedOnL1; }`. This enables on-chain monitoring and off-chain alerting.
findings.status: OPEN — Should implement for production assurance

findings.title: 3-of-5 multisig threshold is hardcoded — cannot adapt to threat landscape
findings.description: REQUIRED_CONFIRMATIONS=3 and NUM_OPERATORS=5 are declared as `constant`. This means the threshold cannot be adjusted if: (1) An operator is permanently unavailable (effectively 3-of-4 or 3-of-3), (2) The threat level requires higher confirmation (e.g., 4-of-5), (3) More operators are needed for decentralization. Combined with M-04 (no operator update mechanism), this creates operational rigidity.
findings.recommendation: Make confirmation threshold a mutable state variable with timelocked updates. Allow operator set size changes (add/remove operators). Consider implementing a more flexible multisig scheme (e.g., OpenZeppelin's SignerManager or a custom threshold+set management contract).
findings.status: OPEN — Governance flexibility required for production

findings.title: L1 release address is an unvalidated string — no format verification
findings.description: initiateBurnRelease accepts a `string calldata l1ReleaseAddress` with no validation. A BAIT L1 address should follow a specific Bech32 format (b'...'), but any arbitrary string is accepted. Operators confirming a burn-release have no on-chain way to verify the L1 address format. A typo or malicious address could result in tokens being burned on Ethereum but released to an invalid or wrong L1 address.
findings.recommendation: Add basic format validation: (1) Check that the string starts with 'b1' (BAIT Bech32 prefix), (2) Check minimum/maximum length, (3) Consider using bytes instead of string for gas efficiency. Full Bech32 validation on-chain is expensive; consider a two-phase approach where operators validate off-chain and only confirm if the address is valid.
findings.status: OPEN — Add basic format validation

findings.title: lockRequestIds and burnReleaseIds arrays grow unbounded — potential gas griefing
findings.description: The arrays `lockRequestIds` and `burnReleaseIds` (lines 41, 54) grow without bound. Over time, any function iterating over these arrays could hit block gas limits. The view functions `getLockRequestCount()` and `getBurnReleaseCount()` are safe (just .length), but future additions that iterate these arrays would be at risk.
findings.recommendation: This is a low risk since current code only uses .length. However, consider: (1) Adding a pagination mechanism, (2) Implementing a cleanup mechanism for executed requests, (3) Using EnumerableSet instead of array+mapping.
findings.status: ACKNOWLEDGED — Low risk with current code; monitor for future iterations

scoring_notes.code_security: Deducted for reentrancy pattern (H-01), unchecked return (H-02), sandwich vulnerability (M-09). Strong supply cap and burn mechanics.
scoring_notes.code_quality: Deducted for missing zero-checks, unindexed events, naming convention issues, incomplete test coverage. Good documentation and NatSpec.
scoring_notes.access_control: Deducted for single-owner pattern (AI-01, AI-02), no timelock on owner actions, hardcoded multisig params. 3-of-5 bridge multisig is well-designed.
scoring_notes.centralization: Significant deduction: owner can freeze all transfers and bridge operations instantly, immutable bridgeLock, no operator update mechanism, no timelocked governance.
scoring_notes.decentralization_impact: Owner can rug via pause, single deployer has temporary mint power, 3-of-5 operators provide some decentralization for bridge ops but not for protocol governance.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: addLiquidity with amount0Min=0 and amount1Min=0 allows sandwich attacks on the liquidity provision. No protection against frontrunning on lock-mint requests, though 3-of-5 confirmation mitigates this.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Set minimum amount parameters. Use private mempool (Flashbots) for liquidity operations.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: When createPool() initializes with INITIAL_SQRT_PRICE, a sandwich attacker could front-run the pool creation with small liquidity at a different price, forcing the initial price to be unfavorable. However, since createPool() checks if pool exists first, and the owner controls the call, this is mitigated by using a private mempool.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Submit pool creation and initial liquidity in same transaction via Flashbots/private mempool.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: Single owner can: pause all transfers (denial of service), pause bridge (freeze cross-chain operations), add/remove liquidity. If owner key is compromised, full protocol takeover is possible. Ownable2Step only protects ownership transfer, not operational actions.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Replace with timelocked multisig governance. Add time-locked pause with auto-unpause.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: Three bypass vectors: (1) Per-recipient limit allows N*100K/day across N addresses, (2) block.timestamp manipulation enables ~15s boundary crossing for double daily limit, (3) Operators could split large mints across multiple recipient addresses to avoid triggering rate limits.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Add global daily mint limit. Use block.number for time approximation. Monitor operator behavior off-chain.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: 3 of 5 operators can mint wBAIT without corresponding L1 locks (breaking the conservation invariant). This is inherent to the trust model. The 3-of-5 threshold provides reasonable security but is not trustless.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Implement on-chain L1 light client verification when available. Add totalLockedOnL1 tracking. Monitor operator behavior with off-chain alerting.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: Owner can call WBAIT.pause() to freeze all token transfers and BridgeLock.pause() to freeze all bridge operations. No on-chain mechanism to unpause without owner action. This is a permanent DoS vector if owner key is lost.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Add auto-unpause timer (e.g., 72h max pause). Add multisig requirement for pause. Implement granular pausing (separate mint-pause from transfer-pause).

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: If WBAIT is modified to support ERC-777 hooks or callback mechanisms, the CEI violation in initiateBurnRelease could be exploitable. Currently mitigated by nonReentrant modifier and no callback mechanism in WBAIT.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Reorder to follow CEI pattern. Document that WBAIT must never implement hooks. Consider reentrancy guard at WBAIT level.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: Users who call initiateBurnRelease without first approving BridgeLock to burn their tokens will get a revert. This is a UX issue, not a security vulnerability, but could be used in a griefing attack where a user is tricked into calling initiateBurnRelease without approval, wasting gas.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Add permit-based burn flow. Check allowance and provide clear error message.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: An attacker could request lock-mints up to the 21M supply cap (within rate limits), preventing legitimate users from bridging. At 100K/day/address, exhausting 21M would take 210 days per address, or 42 days with 5 addresses.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Monitor supply utilization off-chain. Add a minimum bridge amount. The 21M cap itself is the protection — exhaustion just fills the cap with valid mints.

attack_vectors_analyzed.description: The deployment script deploys WBAIT with msg.sender as temporary bridgeLock. If deployment transactions are front-run, an attacker could deploy their own WBAIT with their address as bridgeLock and trick users into using the wrong contract.
attack_vectors_analyzed.mitigation: Use CREATE2 for deterministic addresses. Verify deployed addresses on-chain. Use EIP-712 typed data for user signatures.

gas_optimization.optimization: Use a sequential counter instead of keccak256 hash for releaseId. Saves ~3000 gas per initiateBurnRelease call (keccak256 of 4 words is expensive).

gas_optimization.current: string l1ReleaseAddress in BurnRelease struct and event
gas_optimization.optimization: Use bytes32 instead of string for L1 addresses. BAIT addresses fit in bytes32 (Bech32 is ~42 chars but can be stored as raw bytes). Saves storage slot and avoids string's length prefix overhead.
gas_optimization.savings: ~2000 gas per storage write, ~800 per event emission

gas_optimization.current: uint256 currentDay = block.timestamp / 1 days; if (lastMintDay[recipient] != currentDay) { dailyMinted[recipient] = 0; lastMintDay[recipient] = currentDay; }
gas_optimization.optimization: Pack lastMintDay and dailyMinted into a single storage slot using a struct with uint128 for each. Since max daily is 100K*10^8 = 10^13 which fits in uint128, and day numbers fit in uint128, this saves one SSTORE (~20k gas) on the first mint of each day.

Use infinite approval (type(uint256).max) once in constructor or initialization, then skip approve in addLiquidity. Saves ~46k gas (cold SSTORE + warm SSTORE) per addLiquidity call. Security trade-off: infinite approval to position manager.
gas_optimization.savings: ~46000 gas per addLiquidity call (after initial approval)

gas_optimization.optimization: The whenNotPaused check adds a cold SLOAD for _paused slot on every transfer. Consider using a free memory read pattern or caching the paused state. Since OpenZeppelin 5.x Pausable uses a StorageSlot, this is already fairly optimized.

gas_optimization.current: bytes32[] public lockRequestIds / burnReleaseIds — arrays grow unbounded
gas_optimization.optimization: Consider removing these arrays if they are only used for counting. Replace with a uint256 counter. Saves gas on array push (~20k gas per push due to length update and potential resize).

Pre-compute the 90% threshold as a constant: uint256 public constant SUPPLY_ALERT_THRESHOLD = (MAX_SUPPLY * 90) / 100; Then check: if (totalSupply() > SUPPLY_ALERT_THRESHOLD). Saves one MUL and one DIV per mint.

recommendations.recommendation: Replace single-owner with timelocked multisig governance (3-of-5 + 48h TimelockController). This addresses AI-01 and AI-02.
Implement operator update mechanism with 24h timelock. Add proposeOperatorUpdate() and executeOperatorUpdate() functions. This addresses M-04.
Fix CEI violation in initiateBurnRelease: reorder state writes before external call. This addresses H-01.
Add SafeERC20.safeApprove() or require() on approve return value. This addresses H-02.
Set amount0Min and amount1Min to non-zero slippage tolerances in addLiquidity. This addresses M-09.
Add auto-unpause mechanism and multisig requirement for pause operations. This addresses AI-02.
Add zero-address validation for all constructor parameters in BAITUniswapV3Liquidity. This addresses M-01.
Add on-chain conservation invariant tracking (totalLockedOnL1 counter). This addresses AI-03.
Add amount parameter to initiateBurnRelease and implement permit-based burn flow. This addresses M-07 and M-08.
Add L1 address format validation (prefix check) in initiateBurnRelease. This addresses AI-05.
Make multisig threshold and operator set mutable with timelocked updates. This addresses AI-04.
Add request cancellation mechanism for pending lock-mints and burn-releases. This addresses M-11.
Upgrade Solidity to 0.8.28+ and pin exact version (remove caret ^). This addresses M-06.
Index address parameters in OperatorUpdated event. This addresses L-01.
Implement CREATE2 pre-computation or factory pattern for atomic deployment. This addresses L-05.
Expand test suite to >95% coverage with integration tests, invariant tests, and fuzz tests. This addresses L-06.

conservation_invariant_analysis.enforcement: OFF-CHAIN ONLY — No on-chain variable tracks totalLockedOnL1
conservation_invariant_analysis.mint_path: L1 lock → operator observes → requestLockMint → confirmLockMint (×3) → _executeLockMint → WBAIT.mint
conservation_invariant_analysis.burn_path: User initiateBurnRelease → WBAIT.burnFrom → operator observes L1 release → confirmBurnRelease (×3) → BurnExecuted event
conservation_invariant_analysis.risk: If 3-of-5 operators mint without L1 lock, invariant is broken. No on-chain detection mechanism.
conservation_invariant_analysis.recommendation: Add totalLockedOnL1 tracking and on-chain verification function
